summary: Updates TLS-based EAP types such as EAP-FAST, EAP-TTLS, and TEAP, and possibly PEAP, to work with TLS 1.3, following what RFC 9190 did for EAP-TLS.

plainLanguage.summary: Several ways of logging in to a network are built as a secure TLS channel with a second, inner authentication step inside it. TLS 1.3 changed the way keys are derived, which broke those methods, and this RFC puts them right.

questions: how does teap work with tls 1.3
can tls 1.3 session tickets bypass eap authentication
subtitle: How EAP methods built on TLS, such as TEAP, EAP-FAST, EAP-TTLS and PEAP, move to TLS 1.3.

tldr.problem: EAP-TLS was updated for TLS 1.3 in RFC 9190, but other EAP types that run inside TLS use key derivation functions that no longer apply to TLS 1.3, so they cannot be used with it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9427 defines new key derivations based on the TLS-Exporter, adds the logical EAP Type to each derivation, and spells out the other changes TLS 1.3 forces: how application data is handled, when session tickets may be issued, when client certificates are allowed, which identities to use and how resumption works.
tldr.outcome: TEAP, EAP-FAST, EAP-TTLS and, where applicable, PEAP and vendor-specific methods can run over TLS 1.3. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4851, RFC 5281 and RFC 7170, and it is itself updated by RFC 9930.

today: RFC 9427 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2023. It updates RFC 4851, RFC 5281 and RFC 7170, and it is itself updated by RFC 9930. It follows RFC 9190, which did the same work for EAP-TLS.

sections.title: Why TLS-Based EAP Methods Needed an Update
sections.content:
EAP is the protocol that carries authentication exchanges, and many EAP methods are built on TLS. EAP-TLS was updated for TLS 1.3 in RFC 9190, but other methods that depend on TLS, such as EAP-FAST in RFC 4851, EAP-TTLS in RFC 5281 and TEAP in RFC 7170, were left behind. Vendor-specific methods such as PEAP depend on TLS as well.

All of these methods use key derivation functions that no longer apply to TLS 1.3, so as things stood they were incompatible with it. This RFC updates them. The main change is defining new key derivation functions, and the rest of the document explains the implementation differences that TLS 1.3 brings.

Two differences from EAP-TLS run through the whole document. The first is the EAP Type: RFC 9190 uses the EAP-TLS Type value 0x0D in a number of calculations, while every other method uses its own Type value. The second is the protected success result indication, one octet of 0x00, that RFC 9190 requires after the EAP-TLS handshake. Other TLS-based EAP methods use that indication only during resumption, and not at all for a full authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: Several login methods are a TLS channel with an inner authentication step. TLS 1.3 changed how keys are worked out, and this RFC gives each of those methods the new formulas it needs.

sections.title: Key Derivation with the TLS-Exporter
sections.content:
Each derivation depends on the EAP Type of the method. The RFC defines a logical Type so that the reference is simple: one octet for values below 254, and for an Expanded Type the concatenation of the 0xfe marker, the Vendor-Id and the Vendor-Type. The definition changes nothing on the wire; it only makes the text easier to read. The logical Type for PEAP, for instance, is simply 0x19.

The key material itself is then taken from the TLS-Exporter function of TLS 1.3, with the logical Type as the context. The exporter is called with a label, a context and a length, and unlike earlier TLS versions the length matters, so an implementation must pass the correct length rather than ask for a large amount and cut it down afterwards.

Four values are derived. Key_Material is 128 octets long, Method-Id is 64 octets, the session identifier is the Type followed by the Method-Id, and the master session key is the first 64 octets of the key material while the extended master session key is the last 64. The exporter labels are the ones EAP-TLS already used; the only change is that the derivation now depends on the Type, which keeps it method specific without needing a separate label per method. These definitions apply in full to EAP-TTLS and PEAP, and in part to EAP-FAST and TEAP.
sections.plainLanguage: Every key is derived from the finished TLS handshake with a label, the method's own type number, and a length. Because the length is now part of the calculation, asking for too much and cutting it down gives a different answer.

sections.title: Method-Specific Changes
sections.content:
TEAP and EAP-FAST both used a Protected Access Credential, which does the same job as the session tickets of TLS 1.3 that carry a pre-shared key. The RFC therefore deprecates the PAC for both methods when TLS 1.3 is used, and PAC provisioning is no longer part of either method. TEAP derives an inner method session key with the exporter, using the EMSK or MSK of the inner method, or 32 octets of zero when the inner method gives neither. A session key seed of 40 octets starts the chain, each inner method compound key is 60 octets long and is split into a 40-octet seed for the next method and a 20-octet compound session key. The compound message authentication code is unchanged, but it is now computed with the HMAC algorithm negotiated in the TLS 1.3 key schedule.

EAP-FAST uses the same chain with its own Type, and the T-PRF of RFC 4851 is replaced by the TLS-Exporter. EAP-TTLS derives its implicit challenge for CHAP, MS-CHAP and MS-CHAPv2 with the exporter; the value is 17 octets for CHAP and MS-CHAPv2 and 9 octets for MS-CHAP, and no context value is passed. For PEAP, the PRF+ calculation stays as it is, but the tunnel key must now be taken from the new key material rather than from the older TLS-PRF-128 derivation, and the method defined in the PEAP documents must not be used.

Client certificates are still allowed in all four methods, but a certificate alone is no longer enough: the inner method must still run, and if there is no inner authentication data the EAP server must reject the session. Where client certificates are needed with no inner tunnel method, EAP-TLS should be used instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Each method gets its own adjustments: the old credential in TEAP and EAP-FAST is dropped, the challenge in EAP-TTLS comes from the new derivation, and PEAP takes its tunnel key from the new key material. A client certificate no longer replaces the inner login.

sections.title: Application Data and Session Tickets
sections.content:
TLS 1.3 can continue negotiating after the initial handshake, a state it calls CONNECTED, so receiving a Finished message no longer means the negotiation is over. Earlier TLS versions never sent application data with the Finished message, and implementations relied on that. TLS 1.3 breaks the assumption, so an implementation must check for application data once the session is established, before starting another round of TLS negotiation, and must process that data according to the EAP Type of the method.

Implementations must not send or expect application data while the underlying TLS connection is still negotiating, and must delay processing until the negotiation has finished. If the negotiation succeeded, the data can be examined; if it did not, the data is untrusted and must be discarded without being looked at.

Session tickets need care, because TLS 1.3 lets the server send a NewSessionTicket message after the client Finished message, and many TLS libraries do so straight away. A ticket that works before the inner authentication has run would let a malicious peer bypass that authentication entirely. The EAP server must not let a ticket resume authentication unless the inner authentication has completed, and it should not send tickets until it has. Where a library makes that impossible, the server must invalidate or discard the tickets of sessions that end in EAP Failure. The ticket message should also travel with other application data rather than alone, both to save a round trip and to avoid interoperability problems.
sections.plainLanguage: With TLS 1.3, data and session tickets can arrive before the login inside the tunnel has finished. That would let a client skip the login, so the server must not accept a ticket until the inner login has succeeded.

sections.title: Inner and Outer Identities
sections.content:
The RFC defines the inner identity as the identification information carried inside the TLS tunnel. For PEAP that may be an EAP Response/Identity, for EAP-TTLS it may be the User-Name attribute, and vendor methods usually have one too. The outer TLS layer can be seen as a secure transport that delivers the real credentials to the right EAP server, which then uses the inner identity and the inner authentication data to identify the user.

The outer identity should use an anonymous Network Access Identifier (NAI) realm, which lets the session be routed in a AAA framework and keeps user identifiers private. The inner identity must not use an anonymous realm, and an EAP server must fail the authentication if a peer uses one. Implementations should not put an NAI realm in the inner identity either, since most organizations use a single realm for all their accounts, although separate inner realms are useful when one organization runs several independent sub-organizations.

The routing identifier should belong to the same organization as the data it routes, so an inner identity of "user@example.com" should not be sent under an outer identity of "@example.org". An EAP server that receives an inner identity for a realm it is not authoritative for must reject the authentication. Practices that tie unrelated realms together, such as using a hosted AAA provider's realm as the outer identity or a cloud provider's identity as the inner one, are not recommended, because changing a provider then means updating every device.
sections.plainLanguage: The identity outside the tunnel says where to send the request, and the identity inside says who the user is. The outside one should be anonymous, and the inside one must name a realm the server is in charge of.

sections.title: Session Resumption
sections.content:
Resumption works the same for every TLS-based EAP type, and the only practical difference is the value of the Type field. All EAP servers and peers must support resumption for all TLS-based EAP methods, though a server may still refuse to resume a particular session for administrative or policy reasons, and it is recommended that they enable resumption where they can, because it cuts round trips, latency and load on the server and on the databases behind it.

When a session is resumed, the EAP server must send the protected success result indication, one octet of 0x00, inside the TLS tunnel. The peer must check for it and fail the authentication if it does not arrive. If either side starts an inner tunnel method instead, that method must be followed and the inner authentication must not be skipped.

Although the packet flows for resumption are the same across types, it would be technically possible to authenticate with EAP-TLS and then resume with EAP-TTLS. The RFC forbids this: an EAP server must not resume sessions across different EAP types, and must reject a resumption whose Type differs from the original authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: A resumed session skips the inner login, so the server must still send the protected success byte inside the tunnel. A session may only be resumed with the same method that started it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Moving these methods to TLS 1.3 matters because using the most recent protocol improves the security and privacy of a network. The security considerations of RFC 9190 apply here by reference.

The main risk is the ticket. A malicious client can start a session, collect a NewSessionTicket, abort the session and resume with the ticket, so an EAP server must not assume that a user was authenticated just because a session is being resumed. A server may still run the inner methods even on a resumed session, for example because the password has expired in between. Where tickets are used, the server should track whether the inner authentication succeeded and associate that status with the tickets it issues for the session, either by not sending tickets until the inner authentication completes, by invalidating tickets issued before it completes, or by checking the status when a ticket is used. When a ticket shows that the inner authentication did not succeed, the server must run the inner methods in the resumed tunnel and grant access only on their result. If the server cannot tell the authentication status from the ticket, it must assume the inner authentication did not complete. This does not apply to EAP-TLS, which authenticates the client with a certificate in the TLS handshake itself.

The RFC also looks at the result indications. EAP-TLS provides protected success and failure indications for both full authentication and resumption, while the other methods provide them only for resumption. Most methods do give a protected result inside the tunnel, but inner PAP, CHAP and MS-CHAP do not, because they send credentials with no way to signal the result inside the tunnel. Implementations should replace them with methods that do, such as EAP-GTC for PAP, EAP-MD5 for CHAP and MS-CHAPv2 for MS-CHAPv1, and new TLS-based EAP methods must provide protected success and failure indications inside the tunnel. For PEAP, some derivations still use HMAC-SHA1; the RFC leaves that alone for interoperability, and notes that the data concerned travels inside the tunnel.
sections.plainLanguage: A client must not be able to get network access by collecting a session ticket and resuming before the real login has happened. The server has to know whether the inner login succeeded before it honours a ticket.

viz.caption: What each method changes for TLS 1.3

items.title: TEAP
items.text: The protected access credential is deprecated; the inner key chain is rebuilt on the exporter.

items.title: EAP-FAST
items.text: The credential is deprecated and the old T-PRF is replaced by the exporter.

items.title: EAP-TTLS
items.text: The implicit challenge for CHAP and MS-CHAP is derived with the exporter.

items.title: PEAP
items.text: The tunnel key comes from the new key material, not from the old TLS-PRF-128.

items.title: All of them
items.text: A client certificate no longer replaces the inner authentication step.
